introduction.text: **Before you start.** `RDV-4` gave you the tools of recipe development: ratios, deconstruction, substitution, test plans, writing for others, and a first original dish. Here you use them at scale. You develop at least six original dishes across the categories of a menu, each through at least three documented versions, write them as reproducible recipes, and present them at a tasting day with blind scoring. The six should read as one cook's work: yours.

The course has one template for the portfolio plan (`RDV-5.M1.L1`) and one template for a development cycle, used for every dish (`RDV-5.M2.L1`). The other five dish lessons say what is particular to their category.

items.text: **Original.** Not a course exercise, and not a published recipe with small changes. The dish starts from an idea written in one sentence (`CR-COMP`), and the test log shows how it got from there to the final version.

**Safety.** Assessment §9 applies to every version: proteins to their figures, raw egg and warm egg sauces pasteurised for every guest, preserves by a tested method only, and test portions kept as leftovers (at most 2 days).

**Ingredients.** Dutch seasonal vegetables (velt.nu harvest windows), MSC or seasonal North Sea fish, and Dutch meat and dairy; no imported year-round produce. A dish developed in one season is written with its seasonal window.
**Tasting.** Household panel scores for every version, blind where two versions can be compared. The panel's tasters have taken the salt triangle test (assessment §5.4).

introduction.text: **The point-of-view catalogue.** A point of view is what makes six dishes read as one cook's work:

rows: Season ("one Dutch month, at its peak")
Every dish built on what is best in one or two months
Six dishes that taste of the same two vegetables
Region (the Zeeland coast, the sandy soils of the east)
The region's produce and techniques: mussels, salt-marsh vegetables, rye, buckwheat, smoked fish
Recreating regional classics instead of making new dishes
One technique in a different role in every category
One family explored through every category
A forced use where it doesn't belong

introduction.text: Plan about 38 hours over at least 8 weeks. Each dish's three versions are spread over about three weeks, so two or three dishes are in development at once, alongside `IND-5`.

**Have ready:** the full kitchen of S1–S4; the probe; the 1 g scale; the photo corner (`PLT-4`); the test-plan template and recipe format of `RDV-4`; score cards and coded cups or plates; a folder or document for the portfolio.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. Its one judgment objective (defining the point of view and planning six dishes) is shown in the plan of `RDV-5.M1.X1`, checked against the checklist.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** six good dishes are not yet a portfolio. A point of view, six balanced categories and a test plan for each turn eight weeks of cooking into a body of work that shows who you are as a cook.

**You need:** your record (the dishes and techniques you do best and want to develop); the seasonal calendar; the catalogue above; the test-plan template of `RDV-4.M4.L1`; a calendar for the next eight weeks.
**Explanation:**
*The point of view.* One sentence that says what your cooking is about, chosen from the catalogue or written fresh. Test it: could a stranger tell the six dishes came from one cook?
*The six categories:*

items.text: a starter;
a soup or small plate;
a vegetable-led main;
a protein main;
a bread or pastry element;
a plated dessert.

blocks.text: Together they could form a menu, so plan them for balance across courses (`MNU-4.M1`): no repeated main ingredient, technique or texture.
*Per dish, the plan holds:*

items.text: the idea in one sentence;
the starting framework or ratio (`RDV-4.M1`);
the first version;
the question each test round must answer, and the variable for that round;
how it is scored (household panel, blind where possible);
the seasonal window.

blocks.text: A worked line, for the point of view "the onion family, through the year":

rows: Leeks as the centre: charred, then braised in their own stock
Char before or after the braise?

blocks.text: *The calendar.* The template of `RDV-4.M4.L1` for every dish, and a calendar that spreads the 18 versions over the weeks.
*Cost.* Test the protein main and the dessert in small portions first; expensive items only after cheaper practice.
**Practice:** None: theory only.
**Look for:**

items.text: the six ideas, read together, sound like one cook;
every dish has a first version and a question for round two before any cooking.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Six ideas that are one dish in six forms
The point of view applied too narrowly
Give it a different role in each category
The dessert or bread left unplanned
A plan that needs out-of-season produce
Move the dish to its window

blocks.text: **Safety:** for each dish, the plan names the §9 rows that apply (the protein, egg, fish eaten raw, preserves), so every version is cooked to them.
**Record:** the plan, ready for `RDV-5.M1.X1`.

exercises.title: The portfolio plan
exercises.description: The portfolio plan, using the template from `RDV-4`.

blocks.text: **Task:** define what your cooking is about and plan six dishes that show it: a point of view, six dishes across the categories, a test plan for each, and a calendar.
**You need:** your record; the seasonal calendar; the catalogue; the portfolio checklist and the test-plan template.
**Framework:** the portfolio checklist and the test-plan template from `RDV-4`.

rows: Season, region, technique, ingredient, or your own
Starter, soup or small plate, vegetable-led main, protein main, bread or pastry, plated dessert
Three rounds; one variable per round; panel scores, blind where possible
No repeated main ingredient, technique or texture
Which dish changes if two repeat
18 versions over about eight weeks; each dish in its seasonal window

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Write the point of view in one sentence, with the reason.
For each category, write the idea, the starting framework, the first version, the round questions and variables, and the seasonal window.
Check the six against each other for balance; change any that repeat.
Put the 18 versions on the calendar.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`CR-ORIG` level 3:** the plan against the checklist: a point of view, six ideas across the categories, a test plan with variables and scoring for each, and a calendar. Level 3 was met in `RDV-4.M5.X1`; the plan applies its development discipline to six dishes, and the logs of `RDV-5.M2.X1` show it.

blocks.text: AI review reads the plan against the checklist: *competent* is a point of view in one sentence, six ideas that read as one cook, a question and variable for every round, no repeats across courses, and every dish in its window; *not yet* is a missing category, a round without a variable, or a dish out of season.
**Time:** 2 h.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. It has no knowledge or judgment objective; the test logs, recipes, photos and panel scores are the check.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** this lesson sets the development cycle you use for all six dishes. A starter is a good first subject: small, quick to cook, and honest about balance, so each version shows clearly what changed.
**You need:** the plan for your starter; seasonal ingredients for three versions; the photo corner; the panel and score cards; coded plates for blind comparison.
**Explanation:**
*The development cycle.* The template for every dish of this module:

items.text: **Version 1:** from the idea and the starting framework; cooked, photographed in the corner, scored by the panel.
**Round two:** one variable changed to answer the plan's first question (a component, a ratio, a method, a temperature); scored, blind against version 1 where possible.
**Round three:** the next question, or the same variable refined. Choose the final version by the scores and the idea, not by habit.
**The final recipe:** weights, cues, timings and the seasonal window, in the format of `RDV-4.M5.L1`.

blocks.text: *The test log.* For each version:

rows: Brighter; the panel preferred it blind

blocks.text: *A starter's job.* Small, bright and appetising. It opens the menu, so acid, freshness and texture lead.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Version 1 (60 min).** Cooked from the plan; photographed; panel scores.
**Version 2 (60 min).** One variable changed; blind comparison with version 1.
**Version 3 (60 min).** Refined; the final chosen; the recipe drafted.

blocks.text: Space the versions about a week apart, so you can think between them.
**Look for:**

items.text: each version answers its question, so the log shows why the final is better;
the panel scores rise, or the log explains why they didn't.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The log can't say why a version improved
The starter fills the panel up

blocks.text: **Safety:** a raw or cured fish starter follows the fish row of assessment §9: frozen first, at −20 °C or below in all parts for at least 24 hours. A raw-egg dressing is made with pasteurised egg for every guest.
**Record:** the test log; the photos of three versions; the panel scores; the draft recipe.

**Why it matters:** a soup or small plate concentrates one idea into a few mouthfuls. It tests whether the idea is strong enough to stand almost alone, with only a base and one contrast to support it.
**You need:** the plan for your soup or small plate; stock from the freezer or the ingredients to make one; seasonal ingredients for three versions; the photo corner; the panel.
**Explanation:**
*The cycle.* As in `RDV-5.M2.L1`: three versions, one variable each, the test log, the final recipe.
*A soup.* A base (stock, purée or broth) and a garnish of contrast. The soup should taste of its main ingredient, not its stock.
*A small plate.* One main element and two supports: one for contrast in texture, one for balance (acid, fat or bitterness).
*The variable.* Often the base, or the garnish's texture:

rows: Does the stock help or hide the vegetable?

blocks.text: *Making ahead.* A soup is a natural make-ahead dish, so plan the cooling and storage into the recipe.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Version 1 (60 min).** From the plan; photographed; scored.
**Version 2 (60 min).** One variable changed; blind comparison.
**Version 3 (60 min).** Refined; the final chosen; the recipe drafted.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the idea is clear in one spoonful;
the garnish adds a contrast the base lacks.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Too much or too strong a stock
A lighter stock, or water, and more of the main ingredient
No contrast in texture or temperature
A crisp, raw or acid garnish

blocks.text: **Safety:** a stock or soup made ahead is cooled by the cooling rule (from 57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours, and to 5 °C or below within 6 hours in total) and kept at most 2 days (assessment §9).
**Record:** the test log; the photos; the panel scores; the draft recipe with its make-ahead note.
**Why it matters:** a vegetable-led main is where this program's produce shows what it can do. Built from structure and given real depth, it should satisfy a panel that doesn't miss the meat.
**You need:** the plan for your main; the component table of `VEG-3.M5.L2`; the decision framework of `IND-5.M1.L1`; seasonal vegetables for three versions; the photo corner; the panel.
**Explanation:**
*The cycle.* As in `RDV-5.M2.L1`.
*Vegetable-led.* The vegetable is the centre, not a side without its meat. Build it with the component table of `VEG-3.M5.L2`:

rows: Celeriac salt-baked whole, carved at the table
Brown butter with its roasting juices
Quick-pickled shallots and crisp celeriac skin

blocks.text: *Reasoned from structure.* Choose the method from the vegetable's water, starch and fibre (`IND-5.M1.L1`). Add depth by browning, umami and fat. A dense root takes a long, dry heat that concentrates it; a watery leaf wants a quick, hot method that keeps it bright.
*The written guide.* A short guide to one vegetable group's behaviour (the roots, or the brassicas, for example):

items.text: its structure;
the methods that suit it;
its faults and their fixes;
your dish as the worked example.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **Version 1 (60 min).** From the plan; photographed; scored.
**Version 2 (60 min).** One variable changed; blind comparison.
**Version 3 (60 min).** Refined; the final chosen; the recipe drafted; the guide written.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the panel doesn't miss meat;
the vegetable is cooked to its best texture, and the guide explains why.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A plate of sides with nothing at the centre
One vegetable, large, cooked to its best

blocks.text: **Safety:** if the dish uses dried beans, the bean row of assessment §9 applies: soaked at least 5 hours, the water poured away, then boiled in fresh water at least 30 minutes.
**Record:** the test log; the photos; the panel scores; the draft recipe; the vegetable guide.

**Why it matters:** a protein main is the most expensive dish to develop and the least forgiving of a wrong doneness. Testing it economically, and probing every version, makes the development honest and safe.
**You need:** the plan for your main; a cheaper cut or smaller portion for early versions where the variable allows; the full protein for the final; the probe; the photo corner; the panel.
**Explanation:**
*The cycle.* As in `RDV-5.M2.L1`.
*A protein main.* Meat or fish cooked to an exact doneness, with a sauce and garnishes that serve the idea. Choose the protein's method from its structure (`PRO-4`).

*Testing economically.* Early versions on a cheaper cut or a smaller portion, where the variable allows; the full protein in the final version. But the sauce is tested on the final protein: a sauce built on chicken thigh may not suit a duck breast.

rows: A small portion of the final protein

blocks.text: *Doneness within §9.* Choose the doneness only within the rows of assessment §9. Write the target core temperature into the recipe.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Version 1 (60 min).** From the plan; probed; photographed; scored.
**Version 2 (60 min).** One variable changed; blind comparison.
**Version 3 (60 min).** Refined; the final chosen; the recipe drafted with the target core temperature.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the protein at the exact doneness in every version, with the reading logged;
the sauce makes the protein taste more of itself.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The sauce doesn't suit the final protein
Test the sauce on the final protein

blocks.text: **Safety:** every version probed against its §9 row: poultry to 75 °C or the poultry table; intact meat and fish to 63 °C for 15 seconds; minced meat and offal to their rows; wild game to 75 °C.
**Record:** the test log with every reading; the photos; the panel scores; the draft recipe with the target core temperature.

**Why it matters:** in a bread or pastry, one change shifts everything else, so the discipline of one variable per round matters most here. It is also where the point of view can live in a grain or a technique.
**You need:** the plan for your bread or pastry; flours, fat and leaven for three versions; the 1 g scale; the photo corner; the panel.
**Explanation:**
*The cycle.* As in `RDV-5.M2.L1`, with baker's percentages as the framework (`BAK-2`, `BRD-2`).

*One variable at a time.* The candidates are hydration, the flour, the fat, the proof and the bake. A change in one shifts the others: more whole-grain flour absorbs more water, so a flour change can look like a hydration change.

rows: The flour: 30 % rye in place of 30 % wheat
The new flour, the rest as round 2

blocks.text: *Its place in the menu.* A bread for the table or a pastry element in a dish. It carries the point of view: a Dutch grain such as rye or buckwheat, or a technique.
*Photographs that compare.* The crumb, crust or layers photographed in the corner, cut the same way each time.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Version 1 (60 min active, longer in total).** From the plan; crumb or layers photographed; scored.
**Version 2 (60 min active).** One variable changed; compared.
**Version 3 (60 min active).** Refined; the final chosen; the recipe drafted in baker's percentages.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the crumb, crust or layers match the idea;
the photos show the change between versions.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The log can't explain the change
Carry the grain or technique into it

blocks.text: **Safety:** a pastry element with a cream or custard follows the egg rows of assessment §9: egg-thickened components to 71 °C, cooled by the cooling rule.
**Record:** the test log; the cross-section photos; the panel scores; the draft recipe in baker's percentages.

**Why it matters:** a plated dessert closes the menu and is the dish another person is most likely to get wrong from a text. Developing it and having someone else cook it from your recipe tests both the dish and the writing.

**You need:** the plan for your dessert; the plated-dessert structure of `PST-4.M5.L2`; Dutch dairy, grains, honey and seasonal vegetables; the probe; the photo corner; the panel; a second cook for the final recipe.
**Explanation:**
*The cycle.* As in `RDV-5.M2.L1`.
*A plated dessert,* built as in `PST-4.M5.L2`:

items.text: a main element;
a contrast in texture and temperature;
a sauce;
sweetness balanced by acid or bitterness.

blocks.text: Use Dutch dairy, grains, seasonal vegetables (rhubarb, beetroot, carrot, pumpkin) and honey rather than imported fruit.

rows: Rhubarb poached until just tender; a buckwheat crumble
Rhubarb's acid against the custard's sweetness

blocks.text: *Written for others.* Give the final recipe to another person to cook from the text alone, as in `RDV-4.M5`. Photograph both results in the corner. Watch them cook without helping, and note where they hesitate: each hesitation is a missing cue or weight.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Version 1 (60 min).** From the plan; plated; photographed; scored.
**Version 2 (60 min).** One variable changed; blind comparison.
**Version 3 (60 min).** Refined; the final chosen; the recipe written and given to another person to cook.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the dessert is not too sweet for the panel;
the other person's result matches yours in the photos.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A cue or weight missing from the text
Add it; ask where they hesitated

blocks.text: **Safety:** egg-thickened components to 71 °C (assessment §9); raw or lightly cooked egg pasteurised, for every guest; cooked creams cooled by the cooling rule. Rhubarb: stalks only.
**Record:** the test log; the photos; the panel scores; the final recipe; the other cook's photo and notes.

exercises.title: Six original dishes, developed and written
exercises.description: Six dishes, each with test logs of at least three versions and a final recipe.

blocks.text: **Task:** develop each dish of your plan to a final, tested recipe through documented versions, with a recognisable point of view. Six dishes, each with a test log of at least three versions over about three weeks and a final recipe. The vegetable-led main comes with a short written guide to one vegetable group, and the dessert recipe is cooked by another person from the text alone.

**You need:** the plan of `RDV-5.M1.X1`; the development-cycle template of `RDV-5.M2.L1`; seasonal ingredients for 18 versions, in small portions where the variable allows; the probe; the photo corner; the panel.
*Procedure:*

items.text: For each dish, run the three rounds of the cycle; log every version with the change, the reason, the result, the panel scores and both bands.
Photograph every version in the corner; probe every protein and custard.
Write each final recipe in the `RDV-4` format with its seasonal window.
Write the vegetable guide; give the dessert recipe to another person and photograph both results.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`CR-ORIG` level 4, in part:** six original dishes with a stated idea and a recognisable style, with development logs. The tasting day (`RDV-5.M3.X1`) shows whether guests understood the idea; one dish in the capstone menu, with the defence, completes the row (`CAP-5.R1`).
**`RD-TEST` level 4, further evidence:** six test series of at least three rounds, the changes and results logged, the final version better by blind tasting where it was compared.
**`IN-VEG` level 5, the vegetable-led main and the guide:** reasoned from structure, without a recipe. With `IND-5` and the capstone's vegetable course, the row is complete.
**`RD-WRIT` level 4, further evidence:** six reproducible recipes; the dessert cooked by another person from the text, the result matching.

blocks.text: AI review reads the logs, the photos, the recipes, the guide and the second cook's result: *competent* is one variable per round with its reason, every reading logged at its §9 row, finals chosen by the scores, and a dessert the other cook reproduced; *not yet* is a round that changed several things, a missing reading, or a recipe another cook couldn't follow.
**Time:** 18 h of sessions over about eight weeks, plus logging and writing.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `RDV-5.M3` in the course file, 2 of them safety items. Pass: 80 % and every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a portfolio is read by people who weren't in your kitchen. Writing it as one document, with an honest reflection on your style, turns six dishes into evidence of who you are becoming as a cook.
**You need:** the six final recipes; the test logs; the evidence photos; your bands and the outside bands for each dish; the agreement log of `REV-5`.
**Explanation:**
*One document.* In this order:

items.text: the point of view;
for each dish: the idea, the final recipe, the test log in short, the evidence photos, and the seasonal window.

blocks.text: *The reflection on style.* Answer four questions:

items.text: what do the six dishes have in common (ingredients, techniques, balance, look)?
what surprised you?
where is the style still borrowed?
what are your next steps (a specialisation, a technique to deepen, a cuisine to learn)?

blocks.text: *Honest scoring.* For each dish, your band and the outside band, and why they differ where they do (the `JD-REFL` agreement log of `REV-5`).

rows: I like more char than the panel
A blind re-taste with less char (assessment §3.4)

blocks.text: A reflection names a weakness with evidence (a score, a photo, a log entry), and a next step that addresses it. Write it after the outside bands are in, not before: the disagreements are often the most useful part, because they show where your own palate or eye pulls away from your guests'.
**Practice:** None: theory only.
**Look for:**

items.text: a reader could cook every dish from the document;
the reflection names a weakness with evidence, not only strengths.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The write-up describes the dishes but not the style
No reflection on what they share
Retake the final versions in the corner

blocks.text: **Safety:** each recipe carries its §9 figures (core temperatures, cooling, storage) and its allergen line, so a reader cooks it safely.
**Record:** the portfolio document and the reflection, ready for the tasting day.

**Why it matters:** your household has tasted every version and knows your ideas. A panel scoring blind, before they hear the idea, shows whether the dishes speak for themselves, and a triangle test shows whether a change is real.
**You need:** the portfolio; ingredients for at least four dishes for 4–6 people; coded cups or plates; a hidden key; score cards; the probe; space in the fridge.
**Explanation:**
*The panel.* 4–6 people, asked in advance about allergens and diets (`NUT-3`). Adjust the menu, or keep a dish apart with its own tools, and tell every guest what each dish contains.
*Blind scoring.* Each dish is scored on a card before its idea is told:

items.text: flavour;
texture;
appearance;
whether the idea comes through.

blocks.text: Then tell the idea, and ask whether they recognised it.
*The triangle test* (assessment §5, [S20]). For one dish with two close versions:

items.text: three coded portions, two the same and one different;
served in random order;
each taster picks the odd one out.

blocks.text: With three portions, a guess is right one time in three. A difference counts only if clearly more than a third of the panel find it. With a panel this small, only a large majority is a clear signal: two of six is what guessing gives.
*Acting on the scores.* Change the dish whose scores or comments point to a fault, and note it in the recipe. Write in the log any scores that don't agree with your own band.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The tasting day (3 h).** At least four dishes served to the panel; blind cards collected; the triangle test run; the results written and one change decided.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the panel names the idea of most dishes without being told;
the triangle result is read correctly, including when it shows no difference.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Scores that only echo the idea
Two of six read as clear
Compare with the one-in-three guess rate
Hold hot or cold; watch the 2 hours

blocks.text: **Safety:** dishes held at 57 °C or above, or 5 °C or below, and out of the fridge for at most 2 hours (assessment §9). Allergens asked in advance; each guest told what each dish contains.
**Record:** the blind cards; the recognition answers; the triangle key and result; the change decided.

exercises.title: A tasting day with blind scoring
exercises.description: A tasting day for 4–6 people with blind scoring.

blocks.text: **Task:** present the portfolio, collect honest outside judgement, and reflect on your style. After the portfolio is written up, hold a tasting day for 4–6 people with blind scoring. Set up a triangle test on one dish and interpret it, and write a short guide to tasting.
**You need:** the portfolio; ingredients for at least four dishes; coded cups or plates, a hidden key and score cards; the probe.
*Procedure:*

items.text: Write up the portfolio and the reflection.
Ask the panel about allergens and diets; adjust the menu.
Serve the selection; collect blind cards; then tell each idea and ask whether it was recognised.
Run the triangle test on one dish; interpret the result.
Write the results, the change decided, the agreement between your bands and the panel's, and the tasting guide.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`CR-ORIG` level 4, the guests' view:** the panel's cards show whether the idea of each dish was understood. The capstone dish and defence complete the row.

**`FL-SENS` level 5, the triangle test and guide:** the test set up and interpreted correctly, and the guide. With the calibration of `IND-5.M6.X1`, the capstone form against the guests' cards completes the row (`CAP-5.R7`).

**`JD-REFL` level 5, in part:** the reflection on style and next steps, and your bands against the panel's for every dish. With the agreement log of `REV-5.M1.X1`, the capstone defence completes the row (`CAP-5.R12`).
**`RD-WRIT` level 4, further evidence:** the portfolio as one document from which every dish can be cooked.

blocks.text: AI review reads the portfolio, the cards, the triangle key and result, the reflection and the guide: *competent* is blind cards collected before the idea was told, a triangle result read against the guess rate, and a reflection that names a weakness with evidence; *not yet* is an idea told before scoring, a chance result called a difference, or a reflection of strengths only.
**Time:** 6 h (the write-up and the tasting day).

items.question: Your reflection lists only what went well. What is missing?
items.answer: A weakness or a borrowed element named with evidence (a score, a photo, a log entry), and a next step that addresses it.
items.why: The reflection is candid and specific.

items.question: Your band for a dish is *Excellent*; the panel's average is *Developing*. What do you write?
items.answer: The two-band disagreement, the likely cause (for example the learner's taste for more acid), and what evidence would settle it, such as a blind re-taste (assessment §3.4).

items.question: In a triangle test, what is the chance that a taster picks the odd portion by guessing?
Two of six tasters found the odd portion. Did the change make a difference?
items.answer: No clear difference: two of six is what guessing gives (one in three), so the result does not show the versions differ.

items.question: When does the panel hear the idea behind a dish?

options.text: after they have scored it blind

items.why: Otherwise the idea steers the score.

items.question: A panel member is allergic to celery, and two dishes use celeriac and a celery stock. What do you do?
items.answer: Ask in advance; change those dishes or make a celery-free version with its own tools and stock; label and tell the guest what each dish contains (`NUT-3`; celery is one of the 14 allergens).

items.question: The tasting day runs long. A chilled dessert has been on the table for 2.5 hours. What do you do?

options.text: throw it away: it has been out of the fridge for more than 2 hours
put it back in the fridge for tomorrow

items.why: Assessment §9, 2 hours out of the fridge.

items.question: The panel scores one dish lower than the others and says it is "heavy". How do you act on it?
items.answer: Find the cause (too much fat, too little acid, the portion), change one thing and test it again, and note the change in the recipe.
